introduction: Xenophon, Oeconomicus 9.11–15; brief comparison with 14.3–10. 253 Greek words in 5 paragraphs.

The choice, training, and incentives of a housekeeper follow Oeconomicus 9.11–15, with comparison to 14.3–10. Proposals and questions are course compositions. The enslaved housekeeper’s private thoughts are not supplied by Xenophon and are not invented here.

Read once for the argument, then translate paragraph by paragraph. Use the glosses during the first pass; translate the closing paragraph continuously. Submit your connected English translation using the reading submission box.

The vocabulary panel separates new required entries from review words. Paragraph glosses supply additional reading support; a gloss alone does not make a word or an advanced construction a production requirement.

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Ἰσχόμαχος τῷ Σωκράτει περὶ τῆς οἰκίας λέγει. οὐ γὰρ ἀρκεῖ πολλὰ κτήματα κεκτῆσθαι· δεῖ καὶ εἰδέναι ποῦ ἕκαστον κεῖται καὶ τίς αὐτὸ φυλάττει. ἡ γυνὴ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ περὶ τῆς ταμίας βουλεύονται. ζητοῦσι γυναῖκα ἥτις τῶν ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ ἐπιμελήσεται καὶ τὰ διδόμενα μνημονεύσει.

Ὁ Ἰσχόμαχος τὴν ἐπιμέλειαν καὶ τὴν μνήμην ἐπαινεῖ. τὴν ταμίαν δεῖ τὰ μὲν δέχεσθαι, τὰ δὲ διδόναι, τὰ δὲ φυλάττειν. οὐ πάντας τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἴσους νομίζει πρὸς ταῦτα. ἀλλὰ ζητεῖ τίς τῶν ἡδονῶν κρατεῖ καὶ τίς ἐθέλει πιστὴ εἶναι. τοιαύτην γυναῖκα αἱροῦνται, ἵνα τὰ χρήματα μὴ ἀπόληται.

Πῶς οὖν παιδεύωμεν τὴν ταμίαν; τί αὐτῇ δῶμεν, καὶ ποῦ τὰ σκεύη θῶμεν; τοιάσδε ἐρωτήσεις ἐν τῷ μαθήματι ποιοῦμεν. ὁ Ἰσχόμαχος διδάσκει τὴν γυναῖκα τὰ χρήματα κατὰ χώραν τιθέναι. ἕκαστον γὰρ τόπον ἔχει, ἵνα ῥᾳδίως εὑρίσκωμεν ὃ ζητοῦμεν. μὴ τὰ χρήσιμα ἐν ἀταξίᾳ κρύπτωμεν.

Οὐ μόνον δὲ τόπους ἀλλὰ καὶ τρόπους διδάσκουσιν. ὁ κύριος τὴν πιστὴν τιμᾷ καὶ τῇ ἐπιμελεῖ δῶρα δίδωσιν. ἵνα πιστὴ ᾖ, πειρῶνται καὶ εὐνοϊκὴν αὐτὴν ποιεῖν. ἐν δὲ τῇ τοῦ Ἰσχομάχου διηγήσει αἱ τιμαὶ καὶ αἱ ζημίαι πρὸς τὸ τῶν κυρίων συμφέρον βλέπουσιν. οἱ γὰρ κύριοι τὸν κανόνα τίθενται.

Ἡ δὲ ταμία δούλη ἐστίν. ἡ ἐπιμέλεια τῶν χρημάτων οὐκ ἐλευθέραν αὐτὴν ποιεῖ. πολλὴν μὲν ἔχει χρείαν ὁ οἶκος τῆς ἐργασίας αὐτῆς, ἡ δὲ οὐ τὴν αὐτὴν ἐξουσίαν ἔχει τοῖς κυρίοις. μὴ οὖν τὴν τάξιν μόνον θαυμάσωμεν· ἐξετάσωμεν καὶ τίς κελεύει καὶ τίς πείθεται. οὐ γὰρ ἡ αὐτὴ ἐλευθερία πᾶσι τοῖς ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ ἐστίν. τίνα νόμον θῶμεν, ἵνα μὴ μόνον τὰ κτήματα ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς ἐργαζομένους φυλάττωμεν;

reading.translation:
Ischomachus speaks to Socrates about the household. For it is not enough to possess many things; one must also know where each lies and who guards it. Wife and husband deliberate about the housekeeper. They seek a woman who will care for the household’s contents and remember what is given.

Ischomachus praises care and memory. The housekeeper must receive some things, give others out, and guard others. He does not consider all people equally suited to these tasks. Rather, he asks who controls her pleasures and who is willing to be trustworthy. They choose such a woman so that the property may not be lost.

How then should we educate the housekeeper? What should we give her, and where should we place the equipment? We pose questions of this kind in the lesson. Ischomachus teaches his wife to place possessions in their proper locations. Each thing has a place, so that we may easily find what we seek. Let us not hide useful things in disorder.

They teach not only locations but also habits. The owner honors the trustworthy woman and gives gifts to the careful one. So that she may be trustworthy, they also try to make her well disposed. In Ischomachus’s account, however, honors and penalties look toward the owners’ advantage. For the owners set the standard.

The housekeeper is enslaved. Care of the property does not make her free. The household has great need of her work, but she does not have the same authority as the owners. Let us therefore not admire order alone; let us also examine who commands and who obeys. For not everyone in the household has the same freedom. What rule should we establish so that we may protect not only possessions but also the people who work?

objectives: Form and recognize subjunctives of the assigned -μι verbs, including δίδωμι, τίθημι, ἵστημι, and ἵημι as covered by the chapter.
Connect each form with its principal parts and distinguish present from aorist stems.
Extend Chapter 21 uses with controlled purpose, exhortation, and deliberation practice.
Contrast finite subjunctives with familiar imperatives and infinitives; retain agreement and accent practice.

sections.title: 1. δίδωμι and τίθημι in the subjunctive
body: Athematic verbs do not keep their indicative endings in the subjunctive. The present of δίδωμι retains reduplication: διδῶ, διδῷς, διδῷ, διδῶμεν, διδῶτε, διδῶσι(ν). Its aorist uses the shorter stem: δῶ, δῷς, δῷ, δῶμεν, δῶτε, δῶσι(ν). Do not infer aorist simply from a circumflex.

Similarly τίθημι has τιθῶ, τιθῇς, τιθῇ, τιθῶμεν, τιθῆτε, τιθῶσι(ν), while the aorist has θῶ, θῇς, θῇ, θῶμεν, θῆτε, θῶσι(ν). The indicative aorists ἔδωκα and ἔθηκα do not supply a -κ- to these subjunctives. Identify the stem before choosing “give” or “place.”

sections.title: 2. ἵστημι and ἵημι
body: The present subjunctive of ἵστημι is ἱστῶ, ἱστῇς, ἱστῇ, ἱστῶμεν, ἱστῆτε, ἱστῶσι(ν). The intransitive second aorist is στῶ, στῇς, στῇ, στῶμεν, στῆτε, στῶσι(ν), “take a stand.” The transitive first aorist στήσω means “set something up” in the appropriate subjunctive clause; distinguish it by construction from future indicative στήσω.

For ἵημι, learn present ἱῶ, ἱῇς, ἱῇ and aorist ὧ, ᾗς, ᾗ; plural present ἱῶμεν, ἱῆτε, ἱῶσι and aorist ὧμεν, ἧτε, ὧσι. Compounds make the forms easier to recognize: ἀφῶ, “I may release.” Keep rough breathings and iota subscripts in the forms you write.

sections.title: 3. Middle forms and principal parts
body: Middle subjunctives retain middle endings. δίδωμι has present διδῶμαι and aorist δῶμαι; τίθημι has τιθῶμαι and θῶμαι. The aorist middle θῶμαι can mean “establish for myself” or “adopt,” depending on the object. Voice is a relationship between subject and action, not a fixed English reflexive.

Use a principal-part chain to locate the right stem: δίδωμι, δώσω, ἔδωκα; τίθημι, θήσω, ἔθηκα; ἵστημι, στήσω, ἔστησα / ἔστην; ἵημι, ἥσω, ἧκα. These indicative parts guide recognition, but nonindicative forms may use a different stem shape. Compare τίθεσθαι, an infinitive, with τιθώμεθα, a finite first plural subjunctive.

sections.title: 4. Proposals, purposes, and commands
body: Use the same clause questions as in Lesson 37 with the less familiar stems. τί δῶμεν; deliberates; δῶμεν τὰ δῶρα exhorts; δότε τὰ δῶρα commands a plural audience. δῶμεν is not an infinitive, and δότε is not a subjunctive.

A purpose can have a different subject: δίδωμι τὴν κλεῖδα ἵνα ἡ ταμία φυλάττῃ, “I give the key so that the housekeeper may guard it.” Ask whose purpose the sentence expresses. Describing an owner’s plan does not establish that the person carrying it out chose it freely. Keep historical interpretation distinct from parsing.

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Oeconomicus
body: Return to this work with a new question. In Module III, order helped us examine discipline. Here the same household becomes a place to test responsibility and unequal power. Chapter 9 describes the housekeeper’s selection and training; chapter 14 offers a comparison concerning incentives and supervision. Keep the owner’s managerial aims distinct from the interests of everyone whose labor supports the estate.

The dialogue’s twenty-one chapters move from the meaning of wealth to the organization of an estate. Socrates first questions Critobulus about whether possessions actually benefit their owner. He then recounts an extended conversation with Ischomachus, a prosperous gentleman-farmer, about marriage, household organization, agriculture, and directing other people’s work. The shift lets a philosophical question become a tour of everyday decisions.

Read with two questions in mind: what makes management effective, and whose interests define success? Ischomachus describes his young wife’s education and the work of enslaved people from the position of a male household head. His account gives access to ideals of cooperation and order while also revealing unequal authority. Socrates’ questions invite scrutiny; a speaker’s confidence is not a reason to accept every assumption.

Reading invitation: compare chapter 1 on useful possessions with chapters 8–9 on order, then look at chapter 21 on leadership. Could a person have excellent equipment yet manage badly? The English edition linked below calls the work The Economist. Its subject is the oikos—household, estate, and people—rather than economics in the modern national sense.
Compare a manager’s delegated duties with the authority that the owner retains over the household.

links.title: Read the complete Oeconomicus — English translation

sections.title: Order depends on people
body: The Oeconomicus makes storage, memory, and supervision part of effective household management. An inventory can reveal what belongs where, who receives it, and who is responsible when it is missing. Yet the person keeping the inventory has duties and vulnerabilities that the list itself does not show. Ask who can question a discrepancy and whose account will be believed.

In chapter 9, Ischomachus describes choosing a housekeeper, cultivating her goodwill, and using rewards and penalties. His account evaluates these practices from the owners’ perspective. An efficient system can still distribute power unequally. Responsibility for valuable property does not by itself grant the worker freedom or a right to challenge the owner.

sections.title: Wife, owner, and enslaved housekeeper
body: The wife has an active managerial role in Ischomachus’ description, while the housekeeper is enslaved. These positions must not be collapsed into a generic picture of “women in the home.” The household relies on different kinds of labor and authority, and the dialogue presents them through Ischomachus’ account as reported by Socrates.

We do not have the housekeeper’s own words here. A modern exercise may ask what questions she might raise, but it must label those questions as inference or invention. The reading does not invent a private conversation for her or portray delegated responsibility as consent to enslavement.

sections.title: Read an inventory critically
body: Make a three-column inventory: item, assigned place, person responsible. Add two rules, one protecting property and one protecting the worker from an unsupported accusation. Explain which concerns the ancient owner explicitly voices and which your exercise adds. The inventory is a classroom model, not a recovered document.

Translate the proposals with δῶμεν and θῶμεν, then identify who acts in each purpose clause. Finish by translating the final paragraph without consulting the glosses on the first attempt. Reopen support only for forms you have marked, and revise your English after checking subject and purpose.

questions.prompt: What does delegated household responsibility establish?
questions.answer: A task and authority within an unequal system, not automatic freedom.
Who can challenge blame and whose account is believed.
